families.name: Replay-Based Methods
families.definition: Methods that mitigate catastrophic forgetting by storing and reusing a subset of past data or synthesizing new samples from memory during training.

properties.text: Experience replay reuses a subset of past samples during training to prevent forgetting.
Generative replay synthesizes informative subgraphs or data for rehearsal to address storage and privacy constraints.
Gradient Episodic Memory uses a memory buffer to store past examples and optimizes the model to minimize loss on both current and past data.
These methods are effective in class-incremental and task-incremental settings where some data access is possible.
Replay methods are widely applied in graph neural networks, vision, and language models.

limitations.text: Experience replay may lead to information loss if the buffer is too small.
Storing raw data poses privacy risks in sensitive applications like biometrics or medical data.
Generative replay approaches often rely on graph condensation via distribution matching, which may fail to capture complex structures.
Storage limitations in real-world applications reduce the amount of saved data, causing performance degradation.

families.name: Regularization-Based Methods
families.definition: Approaches that constrain model parameter updates to preserve knowledge from previous tasks by penalizing changes to important weights.

properties.text: Elastic Weight Consolidation protects weights important for previous tasks by adding a penalty term to the loss function.
Synaptic Intelligence accumulates task-relevant information in synapses to rapidly store new memories without forgetting.
Memory Aware Synapses selectively preserve or erase knowledge based on usage frequency and importance.
These methods are model-agnostic and do not require storing past data.
They are applicable in reinforcement learning, computer vision, and federated learning settings.

limitations.text: Regularization can limit the model's plasticity to learn new tasks effectively.
Determining the importance of weights can be computationally expensive or inaccurate.
In federated learning, regularization techniques may not fully address non-IID data distributions across clients.

families.name: Architecture-Based Methods
families.definition: Strategies that modify the neural network architecture to accommodate new tasks, such as expanding capacity or isolating task-specific parameters.

properties.text: Dynamically expandable representations augment feature dimensions with new learnable components for each incremental step.
AdapterFusion learns task-specific adapters and composes them to incorporate knowledge from multiple tasks without destructive fine-tuning.
Hierarchical Prototype Networks extract different levels of abstract knowledge to handle emerging node categories in graphs.
These methods allow for positive transfer and better stability-plasticity trade-offs.
They are particularly useful in class-incremental learning and graph representation learning.

limitations.text: Expanding model capacity increases computational and memory costs over time.
Isolating task-specific parameters can lead to inefficient use of shared knowledge.
Architecture changes may not be compatible with all pre-trained models or deployment constraints.

families.name: Prompt-Based Methods
families.definition: Techniques that learn soft prompts or task-specific vectors to condition frozen pre-trained models for continual learning.

properties.text: Progressive Prompts sequentially concatenate new soft prompts with previously learned ones while keeping the base model frozen.
DualPrompt learns complementary prompts to instruct pre-trained models without buffering past examples.
S-Prompts learn prompts independently across domains to reduce forgetting in domain incremental learning.
These methods are parameter-efficient and do not require retraining the entire model.
They are effective in language models, vision-language models, and graph learning.

limitations.text: Prompt-based methods may struggle to incorporate task-specific knowledge into instructed representations under self-supervised pre-training.
The performance of prompt tuning depends heavily on the scale and quality of the pre-trained model.
In multimodal settings, neglecting interactions between modalities can lead to suboptimal performance.

families.name: Meta-Learning Methods
families.definition: Approaches that train models to learn how to learn, enabling rapid adaptation to new tasks with minimal data.

properties.text: Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) trains parameters such that a small number of gradient steps on new data leads to good performance.
DoubleAdapt uses meta-learning to handle distribution shifts in incremental stock trend forecasting.
Meta-continual learning leverages neural processes to estimate uncertainties in evolving data streams.
These methods are suitable for few-shot and open-world continual learning scenarios.
They can be applied to reinforcement learning, time series forecasting, and graph learning.

limitations.text: Meta-learning requires a diverse set of tasks for training, which may not be available in all domains.
Computational costs for meta-training can be high.
Performance may degrade if the test tasks are significantly different from the training task distribution.

families.name: Federated Continual Learning
families.definition: Frameworks that combine federated learning with continual learning to handle distributed, non-IID, and evolving data streams.

properties.text: Personalized Federated Continual Learning creates adaptive continual learning models for each client in distributed devices.
Asynchronous Federated Continual Learning addresses scenarios where clients learn tasks in different orders and time slots.
Federated Weighted Inter-client Transfer utilizes knowledge from other clients while preventing interference from irrelevant knowledge.
These methods preserve data privacy by keeping data on local devices.
They are applicable in IoT, biometrics, and smart city applications.

limitations.text: Communication overhead between clients and the server can be significant.
Statistical heterogeneity and non-IID data distributions across clients pose challenges for model convergence.
Privacy risks remain if intermediate models or gradients leak sensitive information.

families.name: Graph Continual Learning
families.definition: Methods specifically designed for continual learning on graph-structured data, addressing the dynamic nature of nodes and edges.

properties.text: Continual Graph Learning enables models to incrementally learn from streaming graph data without forgetting.
Experience Replay based frameworks (ER-GNN) alleviate catastrophic forgetting in graph neural networks.
Disentangle-based methods separate structural and feature information to handle emerging multi-relational data.
These methods are crucial for applications like social network analysis, recommendation systems, and knowledge graphs.
They address the challenge of evolving graph topologies and new node/edge emergence.

limitations.text: Graph data is non-Euclidean, making standard continual learning techniques less effective.
Capturing complex topological information while maintaining plasticity is challenging.
Benchmarks for continual graph learning are rare and lack unified experimental settings.

families.name: Multimodal Continual Learning
families.definition: Approaches that extend continual learning to multimodal tasks, such as vision-language models and video analytics.

properties.text: Continual Language Learning extends vision-language pre-trained models to new languages without catastrophic forgetting.
CLiMB provides a benchmark for studying continual learning in vision-and-language tasks.
BMU-MoCo uses bidirectional momentum updates for continual video-language modeling.
These methods handle the complexity of multiple modalities and their interactions.
They are applicable in multimodal foundation models, video analytics, and cross-modal retrieval.

limitations.text: Multimodal data is often unbalanced and noisy, complicating continual learning.
Neglecting interactions between modalities can lead to poor performance.
Resource consumption is high when transferring continual learning methods to large multimodal models.
Lack of unified benchmarks and evaluation protocols for continual learning, especially in graph and multimodal domains.
Balancing stability and plasticity in open-world settings where novelty detection and continual learning must be unified.
Addressing privacy and security concerns in federated and distributed continual learning environments.
Reducing computational and memory costs for continual learning of large foundation models.
Handling non-stationary data distributions and concept drift in real-time applications like traffic forecasting and stock prediction.
Improving interpretability and explainability of continual learning models, especially in high-stakes domains like law and healthcare.
Developing efficient methods for continual learning on edge devices with limited computational resources.
Addressing fairness and bias in continual learning models, particularly in semantic segmentation and human-robot interaction.
